# Nebius announces Oct. 1 GPU price hike for Nvidia-based endpoints

By BORSA Newsroom Published Sep 22, 2026, 2:30 PM EDT Updated Sep 22, 2026, 2:31 PM EDT

Nebius (NBIS) is raising prices on GPU computing endpoints powered by Nvidia chips, effective Oct. 1. Prices for H100, H200, B200, and B300 endpoints will rise 16–20%. The move follows a previous price hike this month, signaling strong demand for AI compute capacity.

results.title: H100 Rental Prices Jump 22% in a Month as GPU Shortage Hits Firms and Labs - Seoul Economic Daily
highlights: - Key summary: Vessl AI, a domestic neocloud company, raised the hourly rate for Nvidia H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39 on the 1st of this month, a 24.7% increase. The price adjustment marks the start of similar moves in Korea after U.S. neocloud firms including CoreWeave and Nebius successively raised GPU rental rates. Vessl AI procures most of its roughly 7,000 GPUs through leasing. According to Ornn, an AI computing trading platform, the hourly cloud rental rate for the H100 rose 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, reaching about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. The impact is spreading to industry and research, with some companies abandoning bids for government-led AI transformation projects because they could not secure GPUs, while universities and research institutes scale back the size of their research.

results.title: Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs
highlights:
Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs

Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs

Preemptible VMs now come with dynamic spot pricing: more flexible access to capacity, better control of costs.

September 22, 2026

A virtualized compute environment creates opportunities for both cloud providers and their customers. One is preemptible VMs (PVMs): interruptible compute for non-critical workloads that runs on pre-allocated, temporarily idle capacity. For the GPU compute market, which is still dealing with a scarcity problem, this distribution model presents an elegant solution. Today, we’re introducing dynamic spot pricing for PVMs: an algorithm that reads available capacity and real-time demand signals from Nebius users to set the price automatically.

...

## How spot pricing works How spot pricing works

The spot pricing system aggregates information about existing capacity and demand signals from Nebius customers, then calculates a spot price for preemptible VMs on a specific GPU type in a specific region. The spot price changes over time and cannot fall below a set price floor. There is no upper limit, so during periods of high demand the spot price can rise above the on-demand GPU-hour rate.

Note

Update, November 2, 2026: this section previously stated that the spot price always stays between a floor and a ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate. We have removed the ceiling. Customers can cap what they pay by setting a max price.

Recent spot price changes, up to 30 days back, are shown in the pricing history diagram. This view is intended to help customers identify typical demand and pricing patterns, so they can make informed decisions about how to time their future PVM consumption.

To see the current spot price, customers can simply create a compute instance and select a preemptible virtual machine. The price is currently updated up to every 15 minutes and is the same for every resource type that runs on preemptible capacity, including Kubernetes clusters and Serverless AI.

...

You can start using preemptible VMs today, and the new tooling and settings are already available. Dynamic pricing itself takes effect on 8 October. If you already use preemptible resources, you’ll need to configure a price setting for them before that date. Look out for an email with more information.

results.title: GPU pricing is increasing across the board, but the severity of those increases varies greatly across providers.
highlights:
GPU pricing is increasing across the board, but the severity of those increases varies greatly across providers.

Take H100 pricing as an example.

In 2026, providers in our network have raised their H100 rates by an average of 31.6%.

However, between these providers, their individual H100 pricing has increased as much as 47.5%, and as little as 13.6%.

Movement in GPU pricing as a whole only tells part of the story.

There is still significant price variance between operators, even those with near identical architectures.

## Editor's note

Across the September 14–21 GPU pricing comparison, no comparable public on-demand GPU price changed by more than 1%. The regional lists below show 111 newly visible price lines, 1 restored listing and 6 listings no longer present. These changes reflect published catalog entries; they do not prove new hardware launches, available capacity or product retirements.

The 111 newly visible price lines are all from AWS: nine for the single-GPU H100 p5.4xlarge in Stockholm, at $7.36 to $7.76 per GPU-hour, and 102 for G7e instances in Jakarta. The G7e entries cover six instance sizes and 17 operating-system or software combinations per size, using NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs with 96 GB each. Their GPU labels and counts have now been verified. Lambda restored one RTX A6000 listing in North Texas. Five Lambda A100 listings and one Vultr A16 listing no longer appear in the regional lists for the September 21 catalog.

OCPI moved independently: H100 SXM rose about 1.5%, H200 10.2%, and B200 7.2%, while A100 SXM4 declined 2.9%. Those are transaction-index changes over the same seven days. The provider-floor charts below use fresh calculations from the preserved September 21 catalog, using verified 80 GB A100 offers for Azure on both dates.
